newsitem.title: BRAZIL: YEAREND - Brazil to accelerate state selloffs in '97.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Brazil to accelerate state selloffs in '97.

text.p: Brazil plans to kick its privatization drive into high gear in 1997, hoping to draw more than $10 billion in private investment through sales of telephone concessions, utilities, mines and other assets.

The federal government, which supplied most of the items for the auction block this year, should be joined by a number of Brazilian states eager to get out of the banking and power utility businesses.

"We're entering a peak period of the privatization program," said Winston Fritsch, president of Kleinwort Benson do Brasil, adding that some of the nation's choicest public assets would be offered for sale next year.
FEDERAL ASSETS UP FOR BID
Brasilia hopes to boost federal privatization receipts to $10 billion in 1997, compared to an estimated $3.75 billion this year.
Brazil's federal government was expected to kick off its 1997 privatization drive by opening bids for Band B cellular service, perhaps as early as January or February.
In March, the block sale of up to 45 percent of voting shares in giant mining concern Companhia Vale do Rio Doce, or CVRD, is scheduled to take place.

The federal government also plans to sell at least a half dozen ports next year, including those in Recife, Maceio and Manaus; the northeast section of the nation's federal railway system; and some of federal power firm Eletrobras' units.
STATES JOIN THE GAME
Brazilian states will also step up privatization efforts next year to rid themselves of inefficient operations and help balance their budgets, analysts said.

Sao Paulo state -- flagging behind Rio de Janeiro, which has already begun its privatization effort -- was expected to begin privatizing its network of power utilities by as early as July. Companhia Paulista de Forca e Luz, or CPFL, is the state's first power unit slated for the auction block.

"There will be a great demand for Sao Paulo's power sector," said Jair Ribeiro of Banco Patrimonio/Salomon Brothers. The state's power firms are worth a total of about $23 billion and will be sold off over several years, analysts said.
Minas Gerais should also be among the states selling off assets next year, with plans to privatize state development bank Credireal.

Rio de Janeiro state kicked off its program in November with the auction of power utility Cerj. Late Monday, state officials were forced to call off today's scheduled auction of state bank Banerj due to a court injunction granted to opponents of the selloff.
Officials said they hoped to reschedule the auction before the end of the year.
"Brazil will compete with Turkey, Ecuador, South Africa, which are also selling telecom assets. That's why the sector's regulations are so important," Kleinwort's Fritsch said.

On the telecommunications front, Brazil took a major step forward last week, sending Congress a general telecoms bill that would create a regulatory watchdog, set broad policy guidelines and authorize the break-up and sale of federal telecoms giant Telebras.

Investors would also keep a close eye on developments in power sector regulations, which are still being hammered out. The British firm, Coopers & Lybrand, is currently working on a plan for a new model for Brazil's power industry which analysts expect will be ready by the first half of next year.
Analysts applaud the privatization drives, but warn that state and federal officials should avoid flooding the market with power privatizations and risk diminishing the value of the assets.
"It is important to have a proper schedule to avoid having all sales take place simultaneously," said Jose Monforte, vice president for capital markets at Citibank in Brazil.
-- Sao Paulo Newsroom, 55-11-248-5412
